newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France, Germany vow no delay to EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France, Germany vow no delay to EMU.

text.p: France and Germany, leaders in the drive to monetary union, vowed on Wednesday that there would be no delay to plans to launch a single European currency in January 1999.

"The timetable for Economic and Monetary Union will be respected. I have no doubt about that," French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told a news conference after a meeting with German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and the central bank heads of the two countries.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the question of delaying the single currency had "most definitely not" played a part in the talks in the central French city of Lyon.
The meeting, one of a regular series between Europe's two biggest economies, took place amid speculation EMU might be delayed to give Bonn time to meet Maastricht treaty criteria.
Economists say they doubt Germany, meant to be Europe's model economy, can cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year as required by Maastricht.
Arthuis said he was confident France and Germany would be ready for EMU, helped by growth in both countries of nearly 2.5 percent this year after a temporary slowdown last year.
"We now have a chance to use our growth-oriented policies to achieve our goal," Waigel said. Talk of alternatives to the euro is "not productive and not necessary", he said.
"France and Germany are firmly committed to cutting public deficits," Arthuis said. "They will respect in 1997 the criteria in the treaty and the timetable.
"This timetable will be respected. We have no doubt whatever on these points and I want to remind you of this forcefully," Arthuis said.
Economists, who had said they would be looking for reassurance that EMU remained firmly on track, said the French and German comments were in line with expectations.
"It sounded like the confidence-inspiring statements we were expecting," BIP-Dresdner economist Marie Owens-Thomsen said.

"The market expected them to get together and slap each other's backs and stress their commitment to Maastricht. They are not exactly going to say anything different," Yamaichi International economist David Brickman said.
France and Germany also reaffirmed their support for an informal stability council to oversee economic policies in the euro-zone after the launch of the single currency.

The idea came under attack earlier this year, notably from some members of the German Bundesbank, who feared it might be used to undermine the independence of the future European Central Bank (ECB). The government has long supported the idea.
"Like Arthuis, I consider an informal forum to be a sensible idea. We agree that this should be an informal forum...like the G7," Waigel said.
This council would in no way threaten the independence of the ECB, to which France was fully committed, Arthuis said.
And though it would be like the Group of Seven in its informality, unlike the G7 it would not make proposals on exchange rate levels, nor include central bank governors.

"From what I've seen of the agreements it's questionable whether it will have any meaningful role," Brickman said. "They've agreed to it, but I think the Germans see it more as a talking shop, rather than anything to seriously impede the central bank's work."
Arthuis said he and Waigel had also agreed on the need for more efforts to get rid of tax anomalies in the European Union which create unfair competition.
He said there should be a code of good conduct on taxation and promised to press the European Commission to take action.
"We cannot tolerate these forms of unfair competition. It is the future of the European Union which is at stake," he said.
Both Arthuis and Waigel said the timing of the decision on which countries could join the euro at its launch would have to take account of French parliamentary elections in March 1998.

The European Commission has already suggested it was likely the decision would be made in April 1998. European Union finance ministers will discuss the timetable for deciding who can join EMU at a meeting next month in the Netherlands.
